St. Mark of Ephesus

Saints

St. Mark of Ephesus

St. Mark Eugenikos · St. Emmanuel Eugenikos

Period
1392–1444 in the cathedral account; OCA gives a different death year
Region
Constantinople, Ephesus, Ferrara and Florence
Titles / vocation
Bishop · Confessor · Theologian
Commemoration
January 19

Introduction

St. Mark Eugenikos is remembered as an Orthodox opponent of the union concluded at Florence. His life is particularly important for understanding the difference between participation in a council and acceptance of its final doctrinal settlement.

Read the published life [1]

BackgroundLife and notable eventsDeath and martyrdomWritings and legacyChronology
Death / martyrdom

Died after illness and persecution; the selected published accounts disagree about the year

Read circumstances and sources

Background

The cathedral account calls him Emmanuel, born at Constantinople in 1392. After his father’s death he continues his education, becomes a teacher, and later chooses monastic life with the name Mark. His theological reputation precedes his episcopal appointment.

[2] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 28, 29, 30, 32, 33, 34

Life and notable events

At Ferrara and Florence the cathedral biography follows his arguments about purgatory and disputed Latin teachings. It depicts an initially conciliatory participant who refuses a settlement he believes compromises the Orthodox confession. The rhetoric and interpretation belong to that Orthodox biography.

[2] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 43, 45, 46

Mouravieff’s nineteenth-century history places Mark’s opposition alongside the Russian metropolitan Isidore’s support for the union. It names disputes over the procession of the Holy Spirit, purgatory, eucharistic bread, and papal authority. The author emphasizes the Byzantine empire’s desperate political situation and the hope of Western assistance. In that narrative Mark refuses the council’s acts, while Isidore later returns to Moscow carrying the union’s decisions. The resulting rejection in Moscow becomes part of the author’s history of Russian ecclesiastical government. This supplies historical context for Mark’s stand, rather than making the nineteenth-century book a contemporary transcript of the debates. Its polemical descriptions remain the author’s Orthodox assessment; the biography does not infer that every Western Christian or every later Protestant personally accepted every disputed proposition.

[3] Public-domain historical edition · Printed pages 77–78, council of Florence and Isidore’s return to Moscow

Death and martyrdom

The cathedral biography describes illness and death on June 23, 1444, after persecution and imprisonment. The OCA’s short account instead gives 1457 and age fifty-two. These published dates conflict; this profile preserves the disagreement rather than silently combining them.

[2] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 52, 53, 55, 56

The OCA remembers his refusal to sign the union and his subsequent opposition at Constantinople. Its printed death year is retained here as a source discrepancy, rather than an independently established chronology.

[1] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 3

Writings and legacy

The cathedral life names George Scholarios among his disciples and describes the later commemoration on January 19. Mark’s importance lies in theological witness and the reception of Florence, not in a martyrdom by execution.

[2] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 32, 58, 61

Mouravieff’s narrative follows the reception of Florence beyond Italy and Constantinople, especially through Isidore’s return to Russia. Mark’s refusal is therefore one part of a wider disagreement about doctrine, authority, and reception. The source’s national and confessional perspective remains visible rather than becoming an anonymous verdict attributed to every historian.

[3] Public-domain historical edition · Printed page 77, Mark’s refusal and the later reception of the union

Chronology

  1. 1438–1439

    Theological opposition at the council.

    [1] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 2, 3

  2. 1440

    The cathedral account describes flight and further persecution.

    [2] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 52

  3. Death year disputed in these sources

    Cathedral: 1444; OCA: 1457.

    [1] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 3
